title: Shoot, score, blame, adjust, wipe
allegory: A training loop is an archer's practice routine: shoot a quiver, measure every miss, trace each miss to the part of the stance that caused it, adjust, wipe the board, write the score down, and now and then shoot at a separate target purely to check.
map: the forward pass, then the loss
trace each miss to the part of the stance that caused it
loss.backward(): a gradient for every weight
adjust the stance, then wipe the board clean
a test target you shoot only to check, keeping no blame notebook
validation under t.inference_mode(): measure, never update, build no graph

chapters.name: This loop, again
chapters.note: for batch in loader: ... haven't I written this before?

cap.1: You will write this loop in almost every chapter: for a picture model, a language model, then game-playing agents. Only the data and the score change.
cap.2: You write it for a ResNet in [0.2], a transformer in [1.1], then DQN and PPO in chapter 2. The loss and the data change; the skeleton does not.
cap.3: The skeleton is framework convention, not a published result. ARENA later refactors it into a Trainer with training_step and validation_step, the form you keep.

cap.1: An archer's practice: shoot a quiver, measure every miss, work out which part of the stance caused it, adjust, wipe the board, write the score down. Repeat.
cap.2: Each round is one batch: forward (shoot), loss (measure the misses), backward (blame each weight), step (adjust), zero_grad (wipe), log (the diary).
cap.3: Order matters: backward accumulates into .grad, step reads it, zero_grad clears it. ARENA puts zero_grad after step, equivalent to before forward, marking the end of a cycle.

cap.1: Round and round: each batch flows through the same stations, and the score peels off into the diary. Everything else is detail.
cap.2: loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y) on raw logits, then loss.backward(), opt.step(), opt.zero_grad(), and log loss.item().
cap.3: cross_entropy fuses log-softmax with NLL for numerical stability, so never softmax first. Logging .item() stores a float; storing the tensor keeps its graph alive.

chapters.name: Forgetting to wipe
chapters.verdict: Omit zero_grad and nothing raises. The loss just gets erratic.

cap.1: Forget to wipe the board and today's misses pile onto yesterday's. You overcorrect more every round, and the score starts jumping about.
cap.2: Skip zero_grad() and .grad keeps accumulating across batches. Nothing errors; the loss turns erratic rather than blowing up, so it is easy to miss.
cap.3: Accumulated grads act like an ever-growing effective batch with an effectively rising learning rate. Deliberate accumulation over k micro-batches is fine: step and zero every k.

cap.1: Now and then you shoot at a separate target just to check, never to adjust. But keep a full blame notebook for every test arrow and the shed fills up.
cap.2: Validation never calls backward, so without t.inference_mode() every batch's graph stays on the GPU. Three clean epochs, then out of memory in validation.
cap.3: Each forward retains activations for an expected backward; with no backward nothing frees them. inference_mode stops graph construction; model.eval() separately fixes BatchNorm and Dropout. You need both.

cap.1: Your diary tells a story. The score starts at pure guessing, drops fast once common words are learned, then creeps. The creep is learning too.
cap.2: A transformer on TinyStories starts near log(50257) = 10.8, drops to the unigram entropy of about 7.35, then slowly learns bigrams. Draw both lines before you tune anything.
cap.3: Uniform output gives log(d_vocab) = 10.825 nats; fitting the unigram marginal floors at its entropy, about 7.349. Stuck above 10.8 means something is broken, often a residual or an off-by-one label.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Same rhythm for DQN and PPO
No trained model, nothing to interpret
Validation: did any of it work?

cap.1: Every model you will ever look inside was made by this loop. Learn its rhythm once and every later chapter is a small change to it.
cap.2: Chapter 2 swaps in new losses and data for DQN and PPO, but the rhythm stays. And interpretability needs a trained model: random weights have nothing to find.
cap.3: Nothing in interpretability applies to random weights. Understanding and steering a model starts with a loop you trust: validated, logged, and read against its landmarks.

coda.title: A toy loop on loss w²: slide the learning rate, then switch zero_grad off

curves.f: ((n) => { let w = 1, g = 0; for (let t = 0; t < n; t++) { g = (zero > 0.5 ? 0 : g) + 2*w; w = w - lr*g; } return w*w; })(round(x))
curves.label: your loop

readouts.label: loss after 40 steps
readouts.f: ((n) => { let w = 1, g = 0; for (let t = 0; t < n; t++) { g = (zero > 0.5 ? 0 : g) + 2*w; w = w - lr*g; } return w*w; })(40).toFixed(3)

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: zero > 0.5 ? (abs(1 - 2*lr) < 1 ? 'settles' : (abs(1 - 2*lr) > 1 ? 'diverges: lr too big' : 'bounces at the same height')) : 'swings forever: old gradients pile up'

caption.1: Slide the learning rate, then switch zero_grad off. With it on, the loss glides down. Off, old gradients pile up and the loss swings instead of settling.
caption.2: Toy loop on loss w². With zero_grad, each step uses only today's gradient. Without it, .grad sums every past step, so updates overshoot and the loss oscillates.
caption.3: Without zeroing, the update is lr times the sum of all past grads: momentum with β = 1, an undamped oscillator. With zeroing, plain descent diverges once |1 - 2·lr| > 1.

Distributed training, which shards this same loop across GPUs

hamming.what: The repeated cycle of batch, forward, loss, backward, step and zero_grad, plus a validation pass that checks it worked.
hamming.when: Every time you train anything: a ResNet in [0.2], a transformer in [1.1], DQN and PPO in chapter 2.
hamming.why: Two of its steps are easy to omit and both fail quietly, so knowing the rhythm cold is how you spot a loop that runs but does not learn.

object.title: The memory shelves
object.subtitle: GPU memory held after each batch: one shelf for training, one for validation.

knobs.label: Log loss.item() (1) or the loss tensor (0)

cap.1: A healthy loop. Training memory rises and falls back every round, so the bars stay level. Validation stays low.
cap.2: backward frees each batch's graph; inference_mode never builds one. Memory is flat on both shelves.
cap.3: Steady state: persistent params, grads and optimizer state; per-batch activations freed after backward.

cap.1: Validation without inference_mode. Every test batch leaves its blame notebook behind, and the bars climb until the shed is full.
cap.2: No backward means no one frees the graph. Memory grows with every validation batch until CUDA runs out.
cap.3: Each forward retains saved activations for a backward that never comes: linear growth through the validation set.

cap.1: Wrap validation in inference_mode and no notebook is written at all. The shelf drops flat again.
cap.2: t.inference_mode() stops graph construction, so validation needs only the activations of the current batch.
cap.3: Stronger than no_grad: inference_mode also disables version counting, so its tensors cannot re-enter autograd.

cap.1: Now store the loss tensor in your diary instead of the number. Training memory creeps up too, just more slowly.
cap.2: Appending loss instead of loss.item() keeps each loss's graph reachable for as long as the list lives.
cap.3: A slow leak: every stored tensor pins its autograd history. .item() copies out a Python float and releases it.

predict.q: You forget optimizer.zero_grad(). What do you see?

options.t: An erratic loss, but no error

predict.why: Gradients pile up across batches, so updates overshoot and the loss jumps about. Nothing raises.

predict.q: Three epochs trained fine, then CUDA runs out of memory on the first validation batch. Most likely cause?

options.t: Validation forward passes build graphs nobody frees

predict.why: Without backward, graphs are never freed. Wrap the validation forward in t.inference_mode().

predict.q: Your transformer's loss sits around 7.3 for a long time. What first?

options.t: Compare it with the unigram entropy; it is a landmark, so keep training
Lower the learning rate straight away

predict.why: About 7.35 is the loss of a model that knows word frequencies and nothing else. Worry only if you are stuck above log(50257), about 10.8.

object.where: Any long-running loop that keeps history it no longer needs: stored graphs, stored tensors, stale caches.
